title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes. Using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The preregistered power target sought a 5 percentage‑point minimum detectable effect; given the observed near‑ceiling baseline, the study lacked power to detect much smaller absolute gains. Representative validator traces and provider audit logs show repair was invoked only three times. Under these controlled emulation and task‑corpus conditions we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline; we report artifacts, analytic deviation (Wilcoxon → exact McNemar for binary outcomes), and detailed execution accounting to support reproducible interpretation.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Systems and survey literature emphasize that operational reliability depends critically on orchestration, deterministic validators, and assurance infrastructure rather than on an LLM alone. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes candidate outputs, an automated verifier checks constraints and safety, and an automated repair loop iterates until the candidate satisfies verifier rules. Despite conceptual support, preregistered, paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is sparse. We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench: a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing (A) baseline one‑shot NL→config generation and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline using the same shared initial candidate. The research question (preregistered) asked whether a workflow‑centered paired benchmark can produce an objective paired binary success metric that reliably distinguishes verifier‑assisted pipelines from one‑shot generation across two simulated topology clusters (edge vs core).
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system papers frame LLMs as components inside broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly emphasize that correctness and trustworthiness are properties of the whole orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution), not of the base LLM alone [Large Language Models for Agentic NetOps and AIOps; Towards trustworthy agentic AI]. Generate–validate–repair patterns are proposed across domains (NL→formal specs, topology compilation, configuration repair) and shown to reduce some classes of syntactic and constrained semantic errors in domain demonstrations, but reported gains depend strongly on task selection and verifier configuration [A Verifier‑Grounded Knowledge‑Based LLM Framework; TopoIntent; PreConfig]. Failure‑mode studies document hallucination, unit/semantic errors, overconfidence, provenance loss, and prompt‑injection risks that motivate external validation layers and provenance tooling [EvalHack; RudriQ Linker; LLM Firewall]. Surveys call for workflow‑centered benchmarks that record provider/validator traces and emulator execution to evaluate rollback and operational side effects; NetOpsTraceBench operationalizes these recommendations with a preregistered paired design and archived artifacts.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary estimand: The study was preregistered (study_id = rX4f7-1; preregistration manifest SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712) and froze confirmatory hypotheses, inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, stopping rules, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The benchmark scope specified 1,200 deterministic tasks split into two topology clusters (edge=600, core=600). Implementation and seeds: Tasks were generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (generator_version = 5.0) with frozen generation_seed values; the requested LLM was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json records requested_model = gpt-5-mini, max_output_tokens = 1500). Execution contract: paired episodes used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation per task shared across baseline and guarded). The guarded pipeline applied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rules; if rejected, at most one automatic repair iteration (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) could be invoked. Deterministic exclusion rules (contamination thresholds, unparsable outputs, emulator failures) were enforced automatically; the missingness plan and sensitivity options were preregistered.
sections.results: Execution and primary confirmatory results: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and produced 1,199 complete paired observations. Aggregated counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv) are baseline_success_count = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149) and guarded_success_count = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196, n10 = 3, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446. Because outcomes are binary and concentrated in concordant cells, the archived confirmatory test used an exact McNemar two‑sided test (p = 0.25) and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples: [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957]. Provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203; repair-stage calls observed = 3 (execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json). Representative per‑episode scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json) and validator traces show validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false for the majority of episodes, explaining the low repair invocation rate.
sections.discussion: Practical interpretation: The aggregated evidence shows no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under the chosen synthetic corpus, validator configuration, and requested model: discordant pairs favored guarded (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) but were too few to establish significance at the preregistered α=0.05 given the near‑ceiling baseline. Two principal, artifact‑supported explanations emerge: (1) baseline performance was near ceiling (≈99.75%), leaving little absolute headroom for improvement relative to the preregistered MDE (5 percentage points), and (2) task‑generator and validator design produced many initial candidates that already satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 checks, so automated repair was rarely invoked (repair = 3). These points are supported by the archived provider audit, repair counts, and representative validator traces. Implications: To assess verifier value more sensitively, future benchmarks should increase task ambiguity or adversariality, vary verifier strictness, and exercise multiple model families and vendor renderers.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench (rX4f7-1) comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→configuration pipelines on 1,199 completed pairs. Under the chosen synthetic corpus, deterministic validator settings, and gpt-5-mini, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success and the guarded pipeline delivered a small absolute increase (≈0.25 percentage points) that was not statistically significant (McNemar p = 0.25; 95% CI includes zero). Archived artifacts (provider audits, validator traces, analysis artifacts) support the interpretation that limited headroom and low repair invocation explain the null result. The run artifacts are archived to enable reproducible sensitivity studies that vary corpus difficulty, verifier strictness, and model families.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct production generalization.
